transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I suppose… what brings me in is that since my wife’s fall, I just haven’t been myself. I used to be the one with the lists, the schedule, the plan—my wife used to tease me about it, actually, said I could organize a hurricane if someone gave me a clipboard.

But now I’ll sit at the kitchen table staring at her medication chart and just… freeze. Sometimes I cry, sometimes I snap over nothing, and then I feel awful. The bills are piling up, the housework’s not getting done, I’ve missed mentoring calls I promised I’d make—things I never would have let slide before. It’s like I can see everything that needs doing, but I can’t make myself function.
Since your wife’s fall, have you noticed that you’ve lost interest in things you used to enjoy, like mentoring or other activities?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I mean, mentoring… I still think it matters. I haven’t suddenly stopped caring about it, if that’s what you mean. It’s more that I get pulled off course, or I look at the phone and think I should call, and then something else—well, not even something important sometimes—just eats up the whole afternoon.

I used to tell my students, “Show up even when you don’t feel ready,” which is funny now, isn’t it? I had one young fellow years ago who would bring color-coded notes to every meeting, made mine look sloppy, and I remember thinking—sorry, I’m wandering. No, I don’t know that I’ve noticed losing interest exactly. I’m just… not keeping up with things the way I used to.
Have you found that things that used to bring you pleasure, like mentoring or other activities, don’t seem to give you the same satisfaction anymore?

I don’t know… satisfaction is a slippery word, isn’t it? I mean, I haven’t sat there after a mentoring call thinking, “Well, that meant nothing to me.” It’s more that I don’t quite get to the call, or I’m distracted when I do.

There was a student years ago who used to send me thank-you notes after every meeting—beautiful handwriting, almost old-fashioned—and I remember feeling so proud of him when he got into his program. That sort of thing still matters to me, I think. I just… I’m not sure I’m experiencing it the same way right now, or maybe I’m too preoccupied to notice. Does that make sense?
Have you noticed any changes in your ability to think clearly or concentrate on tasks lately?

Yes… yes, I think so. I mean, I used to be very clear-headed about things—lists, schedules, checking things off. My wife used to joke I could run the household like a little office.

Now I sit at the kitchen table with her medication chart in front of me, and I just stare at it. I’ll know I need to pay the bills or call someone I promised to mentor, or even just get the laundry started, and somehow I don’t move. Then I get upset with myself, or I snap over some tiny thing, and—sorry, I know that’s not exactly what you asked.

But yes, concentrating has been… much worse. It feels like everything piles up in my head until I can’t function.
Have you noticed that you’ve been moving more slowly than usual, or on the contrary, that you feel restless or can’t sit still lately?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed that in any clear way. Slower… maybe some days I take longer getting around to things, but I couldn’t tell you if that’s “moving slowly” like you mean, or just me getting sidetracked.

Restless, I don’t know. I do get up and down sometimes, but I’ve always done that a bit. My old office had this squeaky chair, and I’d drive people mad with it during meetings—well, that’s not really relevant, is it.

So… no, I don’t think I can say I’ve noticed anything definite like that.
How long have you been feeling this way, and would you describe your mood as depressed most of the day, nearly every day?

About two months, I think… maybe a little more, but two months is the easiest way to say it. It really started after my wife’s fall, when everything at home changed all at once.

As for depressed most of the day, nearly every day… I’m not sure how to answer that neatly. I feel weighed down a lot, but I keep thinking, well, anyone would, wouldn’t they? When the house suddenly revolves around appointments and getting her safely from one room to another… It’s funny, we used to argue about where to keep the spare keys, and now that seems like such a silly thing.

But yes, this has been going on since then—around two months.
Have you been feeling guilty or blamed yourself for things more than usual, or felt like you’re not good enough since your wife’s fall?

I don’t know that I’d put it that way exactly. I mean, I do go over things in my head—what I could have done differently, whether I should have noticed something sooner—but then my mind jumps to practical things, like whether the rug in the hallway is still a problem, or if I remembered to move that little side table.

“Not good enough” is… I’m not sure. I’ve never been someone who sat around talking about self-esteem, you know? My father would have said, “Just get on with it,” which probably wasn’t always helpful, but that was his way.

So… I suppose I blame myself a bit sometimes, but I don’t know if it’s more than usual or if it’s just part of trying to make sense of what happened.
Have you noticed that you take less pleasure or interest in activities you used to enjoy, such as mentoring or other hobbies?

I’m not sure, honestly. Mentoring… I haven’t really thought about it in those terms. I used to like helping people sort things out, especially when they were just starting and didn’t know which end was up. There was one young fellow years ago who kept bringing these enormous notebooks to meetings—looked like he was preparing for a court case, not a project.

But whether I take less pleasure now… I don’t know. Things feel different, but I couldn’t say if it’s that I’ve lost interest or if my attention is just pulled elsewhere. Hobbies, well, I was never one for anything very grand. I suppose I haven’t really noticed it clearly enough to say yes.
Have you noticed that you have less energy than usual or that even small tasks leave you feeling worn out?

I’m not sure I’ve kept track of it that clearly. Some days I do feel… well, older, I suppose, but that’s not exactly new at 68, is it? My neighbor used to say after 60 you start making noises every time you stand up, and I used to laugh at him, but now I catch myself doing it.

Small tasks… I don’t know. Sometimes things feel like they take more out of me, but then there’s been a lot going on, and I haven’t really separated whether it’s energy or just having my mind full. So I can’t say for certain that I’ve noticed a clear change.
Have you found it difficult to make decisions or feel like your thinking has slowed down, even when it comes to small, everyday choices?

I don’t know… decisions have never been my favorite thing, even small ones. My wife used to say I could spend ten minutes choosing between two nearly identical tins of tea, which was probably true. There was this little shop we used to go to—had shelves packed so tightly you felt you’d knock the whole place over just by turning around.

But whether my thinking has slowed down, I’m not sure. I sometimes pause over things, but I can’t tell if that’s my mind being slower or just me being distracted by everything. Everyday choices… I suppose I haven’t noticed it in a clear enough way to say yes.
Have you found that activities you used to enjoy, like mentoring or other things, don’t give you the same sense of pleasure or reward they used to?

I’m still not sure I can say that exactly. Mentoring used to feel… satisfying, I suppose, when someone finally understood a thing that had been muddled. There was a chap once who kept mixing up two departments entirely—sent emails to the wrong floor for weeks—and when he finally got it straight, he brought in biscuits. Odd thing to remember.

But whether it doesn’t give me the same pleasure now… I haven’t really measured it like that. I don’t think I’ve noticed a clear loss of enjoyment. It’s more that I haven’t been paying close enough attention to know.

Would you say that things you used to find meaningful or enjoyable, like mentoring or time with your wife, feel hollow or empty to you now, like going through the motions without really feeling anything?

Hollow… I’m not sure I’d put it that way. Empty sounds very strong, doesn’t it? Like one of those rooms after a house move, when the curtains are gone and every sound echoes. We had a flat like that once, years ago, and the kettle sounded ridiculous in it.

With mentoring, or thinking about time with my wife… I don’t know that I can say it feels like going through the motions. Sometimes I’m not as present as I’d like to be, maybe, but whether that means hollow, I’m not sure. I haven’t really noticed it in such a clear way.

Would you say that things you used to enjoy, like mentoring or other activities, don’t give you any pleasure at all anymore, or do they still feel at least somewhat enjoyable when you manage to do them?

I don’t think I can say “no pleasure at all.” That sounds too definite, really. There are moments that are still… something. Not exactly fireworks, but not nothing either.

Mentoring, for instance—well, if I’m actually in it, talking someone through a problem, sometimes I can still feel a bit useful. Though usefulness and pleasure aren’t quite the same thing, are they? My old supervisor used to say people confuse those two all the time. He had this habit of tapping his pen on his teeth, drove everyone mad.

So… I suppose I’m not sure. I haven’t noticed it being completely gone. It’s more muddled than that.
Have there been times recently when even the things you used to enjoy the most, like mentoring or spending time with your wife, felt completely without any pleasure or joy at all?

Completely without any pleasure… I don’t know. That’s the bit I get stuck on, the “completely.” It sounds very absolute, like saying a cup is entirely empty when there’s still a drop at the bottom, and then you wonder whether that drop counts. My wife used to tease me for leaving just a mouthful of tea in the mug—said it was neither finished nor worth saving.

So, with mentoring, or being with her… I can’t honestly point to a time and say, yes, there was no joy at all. I’m not sure I’ve been keeping track in that way. Sometimes things feel muted, perhaps, or I’m not quite tuned in, but “completely without pleasure” feels hard for me to say.

patient.answer:
Completely without any pleasure… I don’t know. That’s the bit I get stuck on, the “completely.” It sounds very absolute, like saying a cup is entirely empty when there’s still a drop at the bottom, and then you wonder whether that drop counts. My wife used to tease me for leaving just a mouthful of tea in the mug—said it was neither finished nor worth saving.

So, with mentoring, or being with her… I can’t honestly point to a time and say, yes, there was no joy at all. I’m not sure I’ve been keeping track in that way. Sometimes things feel muted, perhaps, or I’m not quite tuned in, but “completely without pleasure” feels hard for me to say.
